title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
summary: Trees turn "search everything" into "walk one path" — and they're the shape recursion was born to walk. Learn five recursion patterns and a third of the interview bank stops being scary.

blocks.markdown:
A tree is nodes connected with no cycles and exactly one path between any two; a **BST** adds an ordering rule that makes search fast.

- **Binary tree** — every node has at most two children, **left** and **right**.
- **BST invariant** — for every node, the whole left subtree is smaller, the whole right subtree is larger.
- Balanced: search, insert, delete are **O(log n)**. Skewed (a line): **O(n)**.
- **In-order traversal of a BST emits keys in sorted order** — the one fact that unlocks a dozen problems.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for it
blocks.markdown:
Pick a tree when you need order *and* fast lookup at the same time.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Sorted keys + ranges | Balanced BST (AVL / red-black) |
| Lookup, order irrelevant | Hash table ([a03-hashing](a03-hashing.md)) |
| Visit in sorted order | In-order traversal |
| Level by level | Level-order (BFS) with a queue |
| O(log n) no matter the input | Self-balancing tree |

blocks.subTitle: Depth vs height
blocks.markdown:
Two words people swap by mistake — they're measured in opposite directions.

- **Depth** of a node — edges counting *up to the root*. The root has depth 0.
- **Height** of a node — edges on the longest path *down to a leaf*. A leaf has height 0.
- The **tree's height** is the root's height.
- With n nodes, height ranges from ~**log₂(n)** (balanced) to **n−1** (a single line).

Search cost is bounded by height, so height is the whole game.

blocks.subTitle: The four traversals
blocks.markdown:
A traversal visits every node once. Three are depth-first, named by *when* you process the node.

![Binary tree with in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order sequences](assets/a08-trees-bst/traversal-order.svg)

- **Pre-order** (Node, Left, Right) — copy a tree, print top-down.
- **In-order** (Left, Node, Right) — on a BST gives **sorted order**.
- **Post-order** (Left, Right, Node) — delete a tree, compute child-dependent values like height.
- **Level-order / BFS** — row by row, using a **queue** ([a05-stacks-queues](a05-stacks-queues.md)), not recursion.

assets.alt: Binary tree with in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order sequences

blocks.subTitle: Traversal template
blocks.markdown:
All three DFS orders are the *same* recursion — only the line that processes the node moves.

```python
def inorder(node):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder(node.left)     # L
    visit(node.value)      # N  <- move this to switch order
    inorder(node.right)    # R
# pre-order: visit BEFORE both calls
# post-order: visit AFTER both calls
```

- **O(n)** time — every node visited once.
- **O(h)** space for the call stack: O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.

blocks.subTitle: BST search
blocks.markdown:
Search is the dictionary trick: compare, then discard a whole half.

![Searching for key 7 in a BST, following left/right comparisons down one path](assets/a08-trees-bst/bst-search-path.svg)

- Start at the root; equal → done, smaller → go **left**, larger → go **right**.
- Repeat until found or you fall off the tree (null = not present).
- Each step drops one subtree, so cost is the **height**, O(h).
- **Insert** is search that doesn't stop — fall off, hang the new node as a leaf.

assets.alt: Searching for key 7 in a BST, following left/right comparisons down one path

blocks.subTitle: BST delete
blocks.markdown:
Deleting a node has three cases — the third is the tricky one.

- **No children** — just detach the leaf.
- **One child** — splice the parent straight to that child.
- **Two children** — replace the value with its **in-order successor** (smallest key in the right subtree: go right once, then left as far as you can), then delete that successor node, which has at most one child.

The successor is the next-larger key, so promoting it keeps the ordering invariant intact.

blocks.subTitle: Why balance is everything
blocks.markdown:
Same keys, two shapes — one fast, one a linked list in disguise.

![Balanced tree of height log n beside a skewed tree shaped like a list](assets/a08-trees-bst/balanced-vs-skewed.svg)

- **Balanced** (left) — 7 nodes, height 2, search ~3 steps.
- **Skewed** (right) — height equals node count, search **O(n)**.
- Real data often arrives **sorted** (timestamps, IDs), which produces exactly this skew.
- **Self-balancing trees** rotate on insert/delete to keep height O(log n) no matter the input order.

assets.alt: Balanced tree of height log n beside a skewed tree shaped like a list

blocks.subTitle: AVL vs red-black
blocks.markdown:
Both self-balance with **rotations** and give the same big-O; constants differ.

| Aspect | AVL | Red-black |
|---|---|---|
| Balance | Strict (±1) | Looser (≤2×) |
| Reads | Faster | Slightly slower |
| Writes | More rotations | Fewer rotations |

Rule of thumb: **AVL when reads dominate, red-black when writes are frequent.** Standard libraries default to red-black.

blocks.subTitle: Tree vs hash table
blocks.markdown:
Both look up fast — they differ on order.

- **Hash table** — O(1) average, but scatters keys; no order, ranges, or worst-case guarantee ([a03-hashing](a03-hashing.md)).
- **Balanced tree** — O(log n) worst case *plus* sorted iteration, range queries, and floor/ceiling.
- Need ordering or ranges → tree. Only single-key get/put → hash.
- Deep tree + recursion → risk **stack overflow**; switch to iterative ([a07-recursion-backtracking](a07-recursion-backtracking.md)).

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Balanced trees run the ordered structures you use daily.

- **Database indexes** (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) — **B-trees/B+-trees**: wide nodes sized to a disk block, so a billion rows is only ~4 levels deep ([b03-relational-db-internals](b03-relational-db-internals.md)).
- **Ordered maps** — `std::map`, Java `TreeMap`, C# `SortedDictionary` use **red-black trees**.
- **Linux kernel** — red-black trees for schedulers and the VMA tree, where an O(n) stall is unacceptable.
- **Filesystems** — ext4, Btrfs, NTFS index metadata with B-tree variants.

blocks.subTitle: Interview patterns
blocks.markdown:
Most tree questions are one of about five recursion shapes — learn the shape, not the problem.

- **Post-order** (depend on children) — max depth, diameter: `1 + max(left, right)`.
- **In-order + sorted** — kth smallest, validate BST via a strictly increasing sequence.
- **(min, max) range** — validate BST correctly; checking locals alone misses deep violations.
- **Walk by BST order** — lowest common ancestor: first node where the targets split.
- **BFS with a queue** — level-order, processing one level per loop.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Validate by checking each node vs its children."** Misses deep violations — carry a (min, max) range or check in-order is strictly increasing.
- **"A BST is always O(log n)."** Only if balanced; sorted input builds a linked list.
- **Depth ≠ height.** Opposite directions: depth up to the root, height down to a leaf.
- **"Successor is the right child."** It's the **leftmost** node of the right subtree.
- **Deep recursion** overflows the stack — go iterative on untrusted depth.
